newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway weighs new investment strategy for oil fund.
newsitem.headline: Norway weighs new investment strategy for oil fund.

text.p: Oil-rich Norway, which now invests its annual budget surplus in foreign government bonds, may soon start pumping its petroleum wealth into the world's major stock exchanges.

The Finance Ministry is thinking about changing the investment strategy for the National Petroleum Fund, which now holds 50 billion crowns ($7.6 billion) and is expected to contain more than 100 billion crowns ($15.2 billion) at the end of the year if oil prices stay high.
The ministry and Norges Bank, the country's central bank, are talking about increasing the risk element in the petroleum fund portfolio now that they seem to have more than enough money to spend.

"As the fund grows in size, and exceeds the buffer that might be needed to finance a (possible) budget deficit, the question of investing in other asset classes arises," Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg said in a recent speech.
According to official estimates, the petroleum fund could amount to 270 billion crowns ($40.8 billion) at the end of the year 2000 thanks to oil and gas production.
Norway, the world's second biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia, pumps more than 3 million barrels of crude oil a day, of which a small part is used by its 4.3 million people.
Years of investment in the North Sea -- which is now dotted with offshore platforms -- have started making their mark on the economy.
Norway began running up a budget surplus in 1995 when two billion crowns ($302 million) were transferred to the petroleum fund, set up several years ago as a "petty cash" for government spending.

The fund was converted last year into an investment fund by the Labour government, mindful that the offshore profits will not last for ever and that the ageing population will be in increasing need of pensions.
The oil wealth is being placed in low-risk government bonds and only on foreign markets to avoid overheating the booming national economy.
But a change in the strategy is expected to be outlined in the revised state budget in May at the latest, officials say.
"Experience shows that expanding the guidelines to encompass also equity capital instruments can yield both a higher expected return and give increased diversification," Stoltenberg said.
While the Ministry is responsible for the fund, the central bank is in charge of day-to-day management.
Leif Eide, executive director of monetary poicy at Norges Bank, is surprisingly open about central bank policy.
"We have few secrets in Norway. Other central banks have been shocked when we told them what we tell journalists," he said.
One of his functions is to keep the petroleum fund money separate from the foreign currency reserve, which amounts to 172 billion crowns ($26.0 billion).
"There is a wall between the petroleum fund and the currency reserve in that the petroleum fund cannot be used for intervening in support of the crown," he said.

Eide said the bank placed money proportional to Norway's imports. Imports from neighbouring Sweden make up nearly 20 percent of the balance, but the Swedish market is small on an international scale, he said.

"This is one reason why we have only placed 5 percent of the reserves in Sweden. The petroleum fund has a longer investment horizon, into the next century, which is why we have 17 percent of the petroleum fund in Swedish crowns," Eide said.
But he cautioned: "This does not necessarily mean that all 17 percent are tied up in Swedish government bonds.
"We might buy American bonds and swap the dollar for Swedish crowns in order to put the currency risk in Sweden. I am not saying we have done this, but swap rates are an option."
Eide said about 18 percent of each fund is in U.S. and Canadian investments.
